practicalQuestion: When workload, wellness, neuromuscular, and schedule-based indicators disagree during a congested week, how should the sports science process account for measurement error, individual baselines, and the cost of false alarms before recommending whether training should be maintained, modified, or investigated further?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate roster with different positions, minutes, and training histories
decisionContext.sport: Team sport using multiple monitoring systems
decisionContext.outcome: Produce a transparent decision-support process rather than a single readiness score
decisionContext.constraints: Missing data; multiple comparisons; limited time for retesting; staff must distinguish group planning from individual follow-up

evidenceConfidence.rationale: Several sources directly address parts of the process: measurement noise against weekly signal, individual baselines, measure sensitivity after matches or during a congested schedule, and bias from missing data. No source tests a process for combining disagreeing indicators into a maintain, modify or investigate decision, so the tier cannot be Moderate. No source tests the cost of false alarms in team-sport monitoring. Most samples are professional or elite Australian football or soccer players, mostly male. The one congested-schedule study had 8 collegiate soccer players, and the wellness and match output study had mostly 6 to 8 days between matches.

dimensions.sourceReview: Original text was checked for every claim. Designs include a reliability and sensitivity study in 42 professional Australian footballers, a retrospective mixed-model study in 34 elite male Australian football players across two seasons, a study of 18 elite football players around 3 preseason matches, a congested-schedule study in 8 collegiate soccer players, a 14-day pre-season observational study in 17 NCAA Division III American football players, a leading article on missing wearable data in collegiate American football, an expert commentary, a framework report, and a laboratory heat-stress validation study.
dimensions.directness: Direct for measurement error, individual baselines and missing data. Indirect for integrating disagreeing indicators, which rests on expert commentary, a conceptual model and one pre-season study linking different load metrics to different recovery measures. Very indirect for false-alarm costs, which come only from a heat-illness warning system.
dimensions.consistency: Sources agree that measures and even items within a questionnaire differ in sensitivity, and that individual responses vary. Wellness tracked a congested schedule in one study but did not relate to subsequent match output in another where matches were mostly 6 to 8 days apart. These studies ask different questions under different schedules, so the tension is largely explained by context but not tested within a congested week.
dimensions.transferability: Mostly elite or professional male athletes in Australian football and soccer. One small collegiate soccer sample, one small collegiate American football pre-season sample and one collegiate American football missing-data example. No female or mixed-sex team-sport rosters, and no multi-system congested-week decision studies.

bottomLine.text: The evidence points toward a process built on each measure's own noise, each athlete's own baseline, and explicit checks for missing data, rather than a single readiness score. Measures differed in sensitivity. In 8 collegiate soccer players, a wellness questionnaire changed more than a single-time-point HRV reading during a congested schedule. In 18 elite football players after preseason matches, FT:CT reductions persisted longer than changes in jump height. In 17 collegiate American football players, different recovery measures tracked different load measures. No source tests how to combine disagreeing indicators or what a false alarm costs in team sport, so those steps rest on professional judgment.

actions.title: Option: know each measure's noise before reading change
actions.text: In 42 professional Australian footballers, sensitivity was weekly CV% divided by test CV%, giving signal to noise ratios from 1.3 to 11.1, with ratios above 1.5 rated good. The authors frame this as a way to identify meaningful changes, those that exceed the noise in the test. Staff could run the same comparison on their own tools and treat changes inside a tool's test error as uncertain rather than as alarms.

actions.title: Option: read wellness against each athlete's baseline and weight items by sensitivity
actions.text: Wellness can be expressed relative to each athlete, as with the within-individual z scores used in 34 elite male Australian football players, whose authors suggest using relative changes to interpret individual responses. In professional Australian football, soreness and stress were the most sensitive wellness items, and the authors advise caution when reading changes in sleep quality, motivation and fatigue. In 8 collegiate soccer players, HRV taken at a single time point changed only trivially during a congested schedule. Those authors note that earlier studies used values from multiple time points and say their result confirms earlier recommendations for a rolling average of at least three weekly time points.

actions.title: Option: pick the more sensitive variable within a test
actions.text: In 18 elite football players from one A-League club around 3 preseason matches, FT:CT from a countermovement jump was a more sensitive recovery measure than jump height, and its reductions persisted at later time points. The authors suggest assessing FT:CT at least 42 hours postmatch to help inform training prescription. Salivary hormones showed substantial individual variability after the acute postmatch response, and the authors question the value of regular salivary hormone monitoring given this variability and cost.

actions.title: Option: audit missing data before trusting the dashboard
actions.text: Wearable data are commonly missing because of equipment malfunction or non-compliance. In 75 collegiate American football players wearing sleep rings, the data likely violated the missing completely at random assumption, response rates fell across the season, and weekend game days were poorly captured, so the data captured were potentially from players who were not traveling. When data are not missing completely at random, averages and dashboards are biased, and the author says practitioners should insist on missing data analyses and imputation as needed. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): record missingness as a reason to investigate rather than as a normal reading.

actions.title: Option: set decision criteria and separate load from response in advance
actions.text: Expert commentary says workload monitoring should assist and inform decisions on player unavailability for training, recommends simplifying reported information, and suggests a clear criterion for proposing player rotations, probably set before rather than during matches. A quadrant model separates load from response and places subjective ratings between the metabolic and neuromuscular domains. In 17 collegiate American football players during pre-season, next-day RSI was influenced by sRPE load while next-day perceived recovery appeared more influenced by mechanical load, and the authors suggest a combination of load and recovery metrics may be needed. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): agree before the week which signals trigger a group plan change and which trigger individual follow-up, to limit chasing multiple comparisons.

monitoring.label: Signal versus noise log
monitoring.text: For each tool, keep its test error next to weekly variation so staff can see whether a flagged change exceeds measurement noise.

monitoring.label: Missingness pattern
monitoring.text: Track who is missing data and when. In the collegiate American football example, missingness rose across the season and weekend game days were poorly captured. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): in a congested week, check travel and game days first.

monitoring.label: Paired load and response
monitoring.text: Pair each load measure with a response measure, for example sRPE load with RSI, or mechanical load with perceived recovery and CMJ FT:CT, so disagreement can be read as load without response or response without load.

guardrails.text: Do not assume a single prematch wellness score predicts match output. In elite Australian football with mostly 6 to 8 days between matches, match-day wellness had trivial effects on subsequent external match load, and the authors suggest that recovery period likely restored wellness. Whether this holds within a congested week was not tested. The same authors still promote wellness monitoring, read relative to each player.

The only evidence on alarm threshold trade-offs comes from a laboratory heat-illness warning system, which reported 98% sensitivity, 81% specificity and 0.12 false alarms per hour at a 38.50°C threshold, and whose authors accepted lower specificity for higher sensitivity in military field training. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): do not borrow alarm thresholds from such settings for team-sport readiness decisions.

limitations.text: Most samples are professional or elite Australian football or soccer players, mostly male. The only congested-schedule study had 8 collegiate soccer players. The collegiate American football load and recovery study had 17 players in pre-season. The wellness and match output study had mostly 6 to 8 days between matches.

The load and response frameworks and the reporting recommendations come from expert commentary and models, not from studies that test decision outcomes. The reliability study did not relate its monitoring data to injury or performance outcomes.
False-alarm trade-offs appear only in a laboratory heat-stress study of a wearable warning system, which does not transfer directly to team-sport readiness decisions.

whatCouldChange.text: Larger collegiate samples, or HRV measured as a rolling average, could change the finding that wellness was more sensitive than HRV to a congested schedule.
Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): local test-retest data showing a low signal to noise ratio for a tool would argue for down-weighting that tool in this team's process.

evidenceTension.text: In 8 collegiate soccer players, the Hooper index (higher scores mean worse wellness) rose more clearly than single-time-point HRV during a congested schedule compared with a low-load training week. In 34 elite male Australian football players, match-day wellness had trivial effects on subsequent external match load, but matches were mostly 6 to 8 days apart, which the authors suggest likely restored wellness. The studies ask different questions under different schedules, so wellness may track accumulated load in a congested week while saying little about output after normal recovery. Whether prematch wellness predicts output within a congested week was not tested.
